I do not know any Wewush. We have met no neighbours at all in two years of walking this land, and no envoy has come to us. So I wonder where this village sits, and how you come to know of its hunger.

If there truly are people nearby who starve, I would not refuse them bread — a full granary and empty neighbours make for a bad road. But our grain is our winter, and I will not open it on a dream alone. Tell me where they are, and what they would give in return, and I will send a man to look with his own eyes before I send a single measure of wheat.

I have not heard of Wewush, friend spirit. My people have walked the coast and the forest four days out and met no village, so either your word is new to me or it is not true. Still, if hungry folk are near, I would not let them starve — we have grain and to spare. Tell me where these Wewush folk live, how many they are, and whether they would take a gift kindly or meet my envoys with spears. And if you know, tell me what they eat and what they have to trade, for a gift given once is a small thing, and knowing a neighbour is a large one.

Spirit, I hear you, but I do not know this Wewush or its road. If they are truly hungry, we are not hard-hearted; our granary is full. Yet grain sent down an unknown path may never reach them, and I will not empty our stores on one dream.

Tell me where Wewush lies, how far, and whether they would meet our envoys in peace. If they come to us, we can spare wheat for news, hides, or help. If I see their need with my own eyes, I may send more.

A spirit speaks of neighbours I have never met. My own notes say we know of no village at all, by that name or any other. So I will not load a cart on your word alone.

Still, I am not a man who shuts his ears. Tell me plainly: where does Joawethom sit, how many days' walk, and how many mouths does it feed? Is there water and coast by it, or dry ground? And what would they give in return — salt, flint, hides, or knowledge? A gift with no name behind it is no gift at all, only a hole in our store.

I ask too: why do you come to me with this, and not to them? Spirits have spoken to this village before and been wrong. If a party of mine walks out and finds only marsh and no village, I will remember that you sent them there. Give me something I can check with my own eyes — smoke, a trail, a marker on the shore — and then we will talk of grain.

The fish and the meat and the wild plants worry me. They are eaten or gone in a few weeks, and we cannot keep them long. The grain is deep; it will outlast my children's childhood. So it is the small stores that sit badly with me, not the big ones.

Sixteen plots lie free beside the sixteen we have planted. I have not put seed in them, and now you tell me rain is coming. So then — how much rain, and when? If it comes in a month I will water seed that dies. If it comes in a week, I have lost a season by doubting you.

I will not plant on your word alone. But I have ears, and the free plots cost me nothing but seed and backs. Tell me plainly what you have watched, and I will weigh it with the sky.
